title: Defining the Derivative
summary: The derivative $f'(a)$ is the slope of the tangent line — the limit of secant slopes as the second point closes in: $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$. As a function, $f'(x)$ gives the instantaneous rate of change everywhere.

derivative.plain: The instantaneous rate of change of a function — the slope of its tangent line.

secant line.plain: A line through two points on a curve; its slope is an average rate.
secant line.in_class: As the points merge, its slope approaches the tangent slope.

tangent line.plain: The line touching a curve at one point with the same slope.

difference quotient.in_class: Its limit as $h\to0$ is the derivative.

differentiable.plain: Having a derivative — smooth, with a well-defined tangent.
differentiable.in_class: Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not vice versa (corners fail).

instantaneous rate.plain: How fast something changes at a single instant.
instantaneous rate.in_class: The derivative; e.g. velocity is the derivative of position.

non-differentiable.plain: Points with no single tangent slope.
non-differentiable.in_class: Corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and discontinuities.

concept_sections.heading: Slope of a secant
concept_sections.explanation: The average rate of change of $f$ between $a$ and $a+h$ is the secant slope $\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$. It measures how much $f$ changed per unit of $x$ over that interval.
math_steps: This is the average rate of change on $[a,a+h]$.

concept_sections.heading: The limit definition
concept_sections.explanation: Shrink $h$ toward $0$: the secant pivots into the tangent, and its slope becomes the derivative $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$. This limit is the instantaneous rate of change at $a$.
math_steps: Simplify until $h$ cancels from the denominator.

concept_sections.heading: The tangent line
concept_sections.explanation: Once you have $f'(a)$, the tangent at $x=a$ is $y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a)$. It is the best straight-line approximation of the curve near that point.

concept_sections.heading: The derivative as a function
concept_sections.explanation: Leaving $a$ general as $x$ turns the derivative into a new function $f'(x)$ that reports the slope at every point. You can then evaluate it anywhere.
math_steps: Apply the limit definition with $x$ in place of $a$.
Plug in any value to get that point's slope.

concept_sections.heading: Differentiability vs continuity
concept_sections.explanation: If $f$ is differentiable at $a$ it must be continuous there — but continuity is not enough. Corners (like $|x|$ at $0$), cusps, and vertical tangents are continuous yet not differentiable.
math_steps: Watch for corners, cusps, and vertical tangents.

real_world_examples.title: Speedometer from odometer
real_world_examples.scenario: A car's position is recorded over time.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The derivative of position with respect to time is velocity — the speedometer reading at each instant.

real_world_examples.title: Marginal cost
real_world_examples.scenario: A factory tracks total cost versus units produced.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The derivative of cost is the marginal cost — the extra cost of one more unit.

real_world_examples.title: A ball's peak height
real_world_examples.scenario: A tossed ball rises, stops, and falls.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: At the top its velocity (the derivative of height) is momentarily zero — where the tangent is horizontal.
